summary: I built and tested a working offline Japanese tokenizer on this machine, so these are measured numbers, not estimates. The firm recommendation is pure longest-match + rule-based deinflection over a prebuilt JMdict index — NOT kuromoji.js. kuromoji's dictionary is 17.8 MB of already-gzipped .dat.gz files (verified from jsDelivr), which is disqualifying for a phone PWA; my index is 1.07 MB gzipped (3.05 MB raw) for all 22,640 common JMdict entries and loads in ~600 ms on this desktop. I ported the complete Yomichan deinflection table (fetched: 36 reason groups, 569 rules, compacts to 20.7 KB raw / 3.6 KB gzip) and it correctly resolves 18/18 hard cases including 食べさせられなかった -> 食べる [causative < potential or passive < negative < past]. Measured on 3,000 real JLPT example sentences: 99.3% character coverage, 0.24 ms per sentence, 122 µs per tap. Along the way I hit and fixed three bugs that will bite the builder if they reimplement naively (a prefix-prune that silently broke all deinflection, cross-length scoring that shattered 日本語 into 日|本|語, and greedy match turning 今日は into こんにちは), and I discovered that YouTube caption baseUrls now return HTTP 429 from this IP even though the player API works — the transcript pipeline needs a fallback.

recommendations.title: Use longest-match + deinflection over a prebuilt JMdict index; do NOT ship kuromoji.js
recommendations.decision: Build a surface-string -> entry-id hash index from jmdict-eng-common at build time. Ship ~1.1 MB gzipped. Reject kuromoji.js, MeCab-wasm, Sudachi and Vibrato entirely for the runtime path.
recommendations.why: Measured: kuromoji@0.1.2 dict is 17,839,010 bytes of ALREADY-gzipped .dat.gz files across 24 files (jsDelivr flat listing), on top of a 41 MB unpacked package — it expands to tens of MB of typed arrays in RAM. My packed common-JMdict index is 3.05 MB raw / 1.07 MB gzip and holds in 25-29 MB heap. kuromoji also gives you morphology but NOT dictionary glosses, so you would still need JMdict on top of it. TinySegmenter is tiny but gives no lemma and no lookup. budoux is phrase (bunsetsu) segmentation, not word lookup — useless for tapping, though see the separate budoux recommendation.

recommendations.title: Port the Yomichan deinflect.json table verbatim (569 rules), not a hand-written one
recommendations.decision: Fetch https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FooSoft/yomichan/master/ext/data/deinflect.json (51,920 bytes, HTTP 200) and compile it to a flat array [reason, kanaIn, kanaOut, rulesInBits, rulesOutBits]. Bucket the rules by the LAST character of kanaIn at load time — that is the single biggest speed win in the deinflector.
recommendations.why: Verified contents: 36 reason groups, 569 rules total, only 4 distinct rulesIn values (adj-i, iru, v1, v5) and 7 rulesOut (adj-i, iru, v1, v5, vk, vs, vz), max kanaIn length 9 (くありませんでした). Groups: -ba, -chau, -chimau, -shimau, -nasai, -sou, -sugiru, -tai, -tara, -tari, -te, -zu, -nu, adv, causative, imperative, imperative negative, masu stem, negative, noun, passive, past, polite, polite negative, polite past, polite past negative, polite volitional, potential, potential or passive, volitional, causative passive, -toku, progressive or perfect, -ki, -ge, -e. Compacts to 20,706 bytes raw / 3,607 bytes gzip. Yomitan's newer japanese-transforms.js (95,408 bytes) is more accurate but is executable JS with a condition graph — 10x the porting work for marginal gain at N5-N1. Tested: 18/18 hard forms resolve correctly.

recommendations.title: Store the index as TWO PARALLEL ARRAYS, never as a JSON object keyed by surface
recommendations.decision: Emit {k:["surface",...], v:[[id,readingIdx,score],...], e:[[kanji,kana,pos,glosses,jlpt],...]} and build the Map with a for-loop over k/v. Do not emit {"食べる":[...], ...} and call Object.entries().
recommendations.why: Measured on the identical data, warm and cold: object -> Object.entries -> Map = 329-336 ms. Two arrays -> Map loop = 75-201 ms. That is a 2-4x cold-start win for a one-line format change. The entries array (flat array-of-arrays, no object keys) parses in only 64 ms for 22,640 rows, which is why the whole payload should avoid keyed objects.

recommendations.title: Do the dictionary load in a Web Worker, lazily, and never on the home screen
recommendations.decision: Put the tokenizer in a dedicated Worker. Start loading it only when the user opens the video reader or the short-story reader. Keep the worker alive for the session. Home / level / flashcard screens must not touch it — they use the small precomputed JLPT word lists.
recommendations.why: Measured full load (parse + Map + POS masks + maxLen table) = 527-669 ms on this desktop (Node 24 / V8, same engine as Chrome). A mid-range Android phone is roughly 3-5x slower, so budget 2-3 s. That is fine behind a 'preparing dictionary' state on a reader screen and unacceptable as a blocking cost on app open. Per-tap cost after load is 122 µs, so interaction is instant.

recommendations.title: Prune the length scan using ONLY the head character — never a 2-char prefix
recommendations.decision: Build maxLenByFirstChar (3,312 entries, built in ~49 ms). At position i, scan lengths from min(14, maxLen[text[i]] + 8) down to 1. The +8 is the maximum tail growth (くありませんでした is 9 chars in, 1 char out).
recommendations.why: I implemented a 2-char prefix-set prune and it silently destroyed the deinflector: 読んでいる, 読んじゃった, 待っとく, 買わなきゃ, 走れる and 働いております all returned NO MATCH, because 読ん is not a prefix of any dictionary key — deinflection rewrites the TAIL, so only the head character is invariant. This is a subtle, high-damage bug that looks like a pure optimisation. Measured: head-char prune alone still gives 0.24 ms/sentence.

recommendations.title: Use strict longest-match; do NOT score across lengths
recommendations.decision: Return at the first length that produces any hit. Rank candidates WITHIN a length by score, but never let a shorter length beat a longer one on score.
recommendations.why: I tried cross-length scoring (rank - lengthBonus*(len-1)) to fix 今日は. It fixed that one case and broke everything else: 日本語 became 日|本|語, です became で|す, ところ became と|ころ, and ご確認いただけますでしょうか became ご|確認|いた|だけ|ます|で|し|ょ|う|か. Single common chars have strong scores and no length bonus survives contact with them. Strict longest-match is what Yomichan and 10ten do, and it is right.

recommendations.title: Block JMdict exp/int entries that END in a particle from auto-segmentation
recommendations.decision: During tokenization, skip a match if EVERY candidate is tagged exp or int AND the matched surface's last char is in {は が を に で と も の へ や か ね よ わ ぞ な さ}. Still return those entries as alternates when the user taps.
recommendations.why: Without it, 今日は友達と... segments as 今日は[こんにちは] — the greeting entry swallows the topic particle. This rule fixed it (verified: now 今日[きょう] は[は] 友達[ともだち]) while leaving legitimate multi-char expressions like 一緒に and につきまして intact. Note it must check BOTH exp and int: こんにちは is tagged int, not exp, so an exp-only check silently fails.

recommendations.title: Add a small hand-written PHRASES layer checked before the dictionary
recommendations.decision: Ship ~300 grammar/keigo compounds (させていただきます, ていただけますでしょうか, なければなりません, ことができる, かもしれない, 恐れ入りますが, お世話になっております, よろしくお願いいたします, ご承知おきください…) as a Map checked longest-first at each position. Reuse the same file as the grammar-lesson data so the reader and the grammar section stay in sync.
recommendations.why: This is the single highest-leverage fix for the user's 'professional/business Japanese' goal. Before: 検討させていただきたく存じます -> 検討 | させていた | だきたく | 存じます (nonsense). After: 検討 | させていただきたく存じます«phrase» with a gloss. Also fixed 恐れ入りますが and ご承知おきください. A word dictionary structurally cannot get these right — no morphological analyzer will either, because the compound is idiomatic, not morphological.

recommendations.title: Treat a katakana run as one token unless the dictionary covers the whole run
recommendations.decision: When the char is katakana, first extend to the end of the katakana run (including ・ and ー). If the whole run is in the index, emit it. Else try longest-match but ACCEPT it only if it covers the entire run. Otherwise emit the whole run as an unknown-but-tappable katakana token.
recommendations.why: Plain longest-match split スマートフォン into スマート + フォン, and would do the same to コンサルティングファーム and テープレコーダー. Loanwords are never partially meaningful. After the fix, katakana misses dropped from 94 to 0 in the 3,000-sentence eval, and every katakana run stays tappable (tap -> offer Jisho lookup when online).

recommendations.title: Make EVERY character tappable with a graded fallback chain
recommendations.decision: Fallback order when a tap lands on an unmatched token: (1) whole-run katakana -> offer online Jisho lookup; (2) kanji run -> per-kanji lookup from the OpenJLPT kanji data (2,211 kanji: onyomi, kunyomi, meanings, strokes, JLPT level) and label it 'probably a name'; (3) single kana -> show it as a particle/fragment. Never render a dead, untappable character.
recommendations.why: Measured residual miss rate is 1.0% of tokens / 0.7% of characters, dominated by proper names (トム appeared 60 times; 成田, 渡辺) and rare kanji (箋, 羹, 膾, 凪). The user explicitly asked to tap ANY word. The OpenJLPT kanji files you already verified cover the fallback with zero extra download budget, and JMnedict (13.4 MB zip) is not worth shipping for this.

recommendations.title: Show inflection chain, JLPT level, reading, POS and alternates in the popup
recommendations.decision: Popup fields: big surface with furigana ruby; dictionary form (only if different) with a tappable 'why' chip showing the inflection chain rendered right-to-left (食べる → causative → potential/passive → negative → past); reading; JLPT badge; part of speech in plain English (v1 -> 'Ichidan verb', vt -> 'transitive'); numbered senses; an example sentence from OpenJLPT; alternate candidates as small chips; and one big primary 'Save to my words' button. Save the entry id plus the surface as seen, so review shows the real sentence context.
recommendations.why: The inflection chain is free — my deinflector already returns it as an ordered array — and it is the single most educational field in the popup, because it teaches the conjugation that confused the learner. Verified output for 食べさせられなかった: {dictForm:'食べる', reading:'たべる', pos:['v1','vt'], jlpt:'N5', inflection:['causative','potential or passive','negative','past'], senses:['to eat','to live on (e.g. a salary); to live off; to subsist on']}.

recommendations.title: Generate furigana by okurigana anchoring, and handle inflected surfaces separately
recommendations.decision: Two functions. furigana(word, reading): walk the word; kana chars must match the reading and consume one char each; for each kanji run, find the following okurigana block in the reading using indexOf(tail, ri + runLength) and assign everything between. furiganaInflected(surface, dictForm, dictReading): take the longest common prefix of surface and dictForm as the stem, strip the dropped dict tail off the reading, run furigana() on the stem, then append the inflected tail as plain text.
recommendations.why: Tested and correct on 食べる->食[た]べる, 引っ越し->引[ひ]っ越[こ]し, 書き込む->書[か]き込[こ]む, 話し合う->話[はな]し合[あ]う, お問い合わせ->お問[と]い合[あ]わせ, 大人->大人[おとな]. The indexOf offset of ri+runLength is load-bearing: without it, 取り引き mis-splits because り appears inside the reading. Whole-sentence output verified: 彼女[かのじょ]は毎日[まいにち]会社[かいしゃ]まで歩[ある]いて行[い]きます。 The inflected variant is required — naive alignment produced 起きて[おきる] and 行[ぎょう]かなかった. Where alignment is ambiguous (compound jukujiro like 日本語, 一日中) both functions bail to a single ruby over the whole run, which is always correct even if less granular. Render with <ruby><rt>; make it a per-user toggle (off / kanji-only / always).

recommendations.title: Split the payload: index.json loads for reading, entries.json loads for tapping
recommendations.decision: Serve index (surface -> postings, 1.17 MB raw / 0.33 MB gzip) and entries (glosses, 2.07 MB raw / 0.76 MB gzip) as separate files. The tokenizer needs only the index to segment and render ruby; glosses are needed only when a popup opens.
recommendations.why: Measured separately: index parse+Map 404 ms (object form) or ~150 ms (array form), entries parse only 64 ms. Splitting lets the subtitle render start before glosses arrive, and lets you cache them under different service-worker strategies. Both go in the SW precache so the app is fully offline after first run.

recommendations.title: Cap glosses at 4 senses x 5 glosses at build time
recommendations.decision: Truncate to the first 4 senses and first 5 glosses per sense when building entries.json.
recommendations.why: Measured: all senses = 3.05 MB raw / 1.07 MB gzip; <=3 senses <=4 glosses = 2.84 / 0.98; <=2 senses <=3 glosses = 2.66 / 0.91. The curve flattens fast, so aggressive trimming costs learning value for little gain. 4x5 is the sweet spot. For comparison, the FULL (non-common) JMdict is 29.5 MB raw / 10.0 MB gzip for 218,776 entries — do not ship it; route rare-word taps to the Jisho API when online.

recommendations.title: Precompute a ranking score per (surface, entry) at build time
recommendations.decision: score = (0 if that specific kanji/kana form is JMdict-common else 40) + 3*formIndex + (25 if it is a kana spelling of a word that has kanji) - JLPT bonus (N5 -30, N4 -24, N3 -18, N2 -12, N1 -6) - 100 for a function-word whitelist. Sort postings by score at build time. At runtime add 8 per inflection step and 16 for exp.
recommendations.why: Without scoring, は resolved to はね and が to え (homograph noise), and 彼 read あれ instead of かれ. With it, particles and JLPT words win, which is exactly right for a learner app. Doing it at build time means the runtime sort is over an already-near-sorted 3-element-stride array. JLPT tagging came free from the OpenJLPT files: 14,008 keys matched 8,516 of 22,640 entries.

recommendations.title: Store the reading INDEX in each posting, not just the entry
recommendations.decision: Postings are flat triples [entryId, readingIdx, score]. Compute readingIdx at build time from JMdict's kana[].appliesToKanji field.
recommendations.why: JMdict entries routinely carry several kana forms that apply to different kanji spellings. Taking kana[0] blindly produced wrong readings in my first build (は -> はね). appliesToKanji is ['*'] or an explicit list; resolving it at build time costs nothing at runtime and a flat triple array parses far faster than nested arrays.

recommendations.title: Add pitch accent as a lazily-loaded optional file
recommendations.decision: Fetch https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mifunetoshiro/kanjium/master/data/source_files/raw/accents.txt (3.2 MB, 124,137 lines, TSV: word \t reading \t comma-separated accent positions), filter to surfaces present in your index, ship as a separate lazy file keyed 'word・reading'.
recommendations.why: Verified: HTTP 200, and filtering to my index keeps 39,787 of 124,137 entries = 1,074 KB raw / 253 KB gzip. Too big to bundle with the core, small enough as an opt-in download from settings. Pitch accent is the thing that separates 'understandable' from 'native-sounding' and is invisible in every free app, so it is a real differentiator — but it is a nice-to-have for N5.

recommendations.title: Use budoux only for subtitle LINE WRAPPING, not for lookup
recommendations.decision: Ship the budoux-ja bundle (small: the ja bundle's source map is 91 KB, so the minified JS is roughly 45 KB) and use it to insert wbr/CSS break opportunities so big subtitles wrap at phrase boundaries instead of mid-word.
recommendations.why: Japanese has no spaces, so a big-font subtitle on a phone wraps at arbitrary characters and looks broken. budoux is Google's tiny bunsetsu segmenter built exactly for this. It cannot do lookup (no lemma, no dictionary), so it complements rather than replaces the tokenizer. This directly serves the user's 'BIG subtitles' requirement.

recommendations.title: Have a non-YouTube fallback for transcripts, and cache raw JSON in the repo
recommendations.decision: Fetch transcripts with yt-dlp (which handles PO tokens and cookies) rather than raw curl, commit the resulting cue JSON into the repo as data, and support hand-authored cue files so the app works even if every automated route breaks. Also pre-tokenize cues at build time and cache the token arrays.
recommendations.why: I verified the youtubei/v1/player call works (returned 'JLPT N5 Grammar - N5 文法 日本語能力試験' with track list [('fr','manual'),('ja','asr')]), but every attempt to fetch the caption baseUrl returned HTTP 429 with Google's 'Sorry...' interstitial — plain, with fmt=json3, and with an Android UA. The bare /api/timedtext endpoint also returned 429, not 0 bytes. So the orchestrator's recipe is half-broken from this IP. Since transcripts must be baked in at build time anyway (CORS blocks runtime fetch), committing them is strictly better than depending on a flaky endpoint. Note the ja tracks on these JLPT videos are all 'asr' (auto-generated): expect no punctuation and occasional garbage, so budget for manual cleanup.

recommendations.title: Pre-tokenize all bundled Japanese text at build time
recommendations.decision: Run the tokenizer in Node during the build over every subtitle cue and short story, and ship the token arrays alongside the text. The runtime tokenizer then only runs for text the build could not see.
recommendations.why: Measured 0.24 ms/sentence, so a 400-cue video is ~100 ms of work — not fatal, but pre-tokenizing means the reader screen can render instantly without waiting for the 2-3 s worker load, and the worker can warm up in the background for taps. It also lets the build flag and fix bad segmentations before a learner ever sees them.

verified_facts.evidence: Corpus: 12,196 unique example sentences extracted from the OpenJLPT n1-n5 vocab files, first 3,000 used. Result: 12,770 tokens, 23,936 Japanese characters, 99.3% of characters covered by a dictionary/phrase/katakana match, 128 unmatched tokens (1.0%), of which 51 were kanji runs flagged 'name?' and 0 were katakana. Remaining misses are proper names (成田, 渡辺), rare kanji (箋, 羹, 膾, 凪, 狂) and stray kana fragments.

Full dictionary load (JSON.parse + Map build + POS mask precompute + maxLen table) = 527-669 ms across runs, heap 25-29 MB. A mid-range phone is roughly 3-5x slower, so budget ~2-3 s cold load, ~0.5 ms per tap, ~1 ms per subtitle line.

verified_facts.claim: Furigana okurigana-anchoring alignment works on real words
verified_facts.evidence: 食べる/たべる -> 食[た]べる; 引っ越し/ひっこし -> 引[ひ]っ越[こ]し; 取り引き/とりひき -> 取[と]り引[ひ]き; 書き込む/かきこむ -> 書[か]き込[こ]む; 話し合う/はなしあう -> 話[はな]し合[あ]う; お問い合わせ/おといあわせ -> お問[と]い合[あ]わせ; 申し訳ありません -> 申[もう]し訳[わけ]ありません; 大人/おとな -> 大人[おとな] (correctly bails to whole-run). Whole-sentence ruby verified: 彼女[かのじょ]は毎日[まいにち]会社[かいしゃ]まで歩[ある]いて行[い]きます。

verified_facts.claim: The kanjium pitch accent dataset is fetchable and filters to a shippable size
verified_facts.evidence: curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mifunetoshiro/kanjium/master/data/source_files/raw/accents.txt -> HTTP 200, 3,226,405 bytes, 124,137 lines. Format is TSV: word \t reading \t comma-separated accent positions (e.g. '１\tひと\t0,2'). Filtered to surfaces present in my index: 39,787 entries = 1,074 KB raw / 253 KB gzip.

verified_facts.claim: YouTube caption CONTENT fetching is blocked from this machine (HTTP 429), though the player API works
verified_facts.evidence: POST youtubei/v1/player with the ANDROID client succeeded and returned real metadata: 'JLPT N5 Grammar - N5 文法 日本語能力試験' tracks [('fr','manual'),('ja','asr')]; '【日本語の森】N5N4 Adjectives and Verbs 45min' tracks [('ja','asr')]; 'Carl Sagan - Pale Blue Dot' tracks [('en','asr')]. But GET on the returned captionTracks[].baseUrl returned HTTP 429, 1,103 bytes of Google 'Sorry...' HTML — identically with &fmt=json3, with a plain GET, and with an Android User-Agent. verified_facts.claim: OpenJLPT vocab files are a usable source of both JLPT tags and 12,196 example sentences
verified_facts.evidence: Downloaded n5 222,308 / n4 218,895 / n3 679,580 / n2 680,482 / n1 1,311,444 bytes, all HTTP 200. Yielded 14,008 distinct word/reading keys, which tagged 8,516 of the 22,640 common JMdict entries with a JLPT level, and 12,196 unique Japanese example sentences used as my evaluation corpus.

risks: A 2-character prefix prune looks like an obvious optimisation and silently destroys the deinflector. I shipped one and 読んでいる, 読んじゃった, 待っとく, 買わなきゃ, 走れる and 働いております all returned NO MATCH, with no error — deinflection rewrites the tail, so 読ん is not a prefix of any dictionary key. Only the HEAD character is invariant under deinflection. Prune on that alone.

Scoring across match lengths to fix one bad case shatters everything else. My attempt fixed 今日は and simultaneously turned 日本語 into 日|本|語, です into で|す, ところ into と|ころ, and ご確認いただけますでしょうか into ten fragments. Use strict longest-match and fix specific bad cases with specific rules.

The exp/int distinction matters and an exp-only check fails silently. こんにちは (今日は) is tagged int, not exp, so checking only partOfSpeech.includes('exp') leaves 今日は友達と... segmenting as こんにちは. Check both.

Taking kana[0] as the reading is wrong and produces confidently incorrect furigana. JMdict entries carry multiple kana forms with an appliesToKanji field; ignoring it gave me は -> はね, が -> え, 彼 -> あれ. Resolve the reading index at build time.

Loading the dictionary on app open will make the app feel broken on a phone. 527-669 ms measured here means 2-3 s on a mid-range Android. Load lazily, in a Worker, only on reader screens, behind a visible state.

Shipping the full JMdict is tempting and wrong: 29.5 MB raw / 10 MB gzip, and iOS Safari's storage eviction is aggressive for PWAs. Ship common-only (1.1 MB gzip) and route rare words to the Jisho API when online.

Naive furigana on an inflected surface produces wrong readings that a beginner will memorise. Attaching the dictionary reading to the surface gave 起きて[おきる] and 行[ぎょう]かなかった. Always strip the dropped dict tail from the reading first, and bail to whole-word ruby rather than guess.
Greedy longest-match will split katakana loanwords into meaningless halves (スマートフォン -> スマート + フォン, コンサルティングファーム, テープレコーダー). Handle the katakana run as a unit before consulting the dictionary.

No word dictionary and no morphological analyzer can segment keigo compounds correctly — させていただきたく存じます is idiomatic, not morphological. Without a hand-written phrase layer the 'professional Japanese' half of the app produces nonsense. This is a data problem, not an algorithm problem.

YouTube caption content fetching returns HTTP 429 from this machine even though the player API works, contradicting the shared context. Do not build the pipeline assuming curl works; use yt-dlp and commit the cue files. Also note every ja track on the JLPT channels I probed is auto-generated ASR, so quality is poor and unpunctuated.

Yomichan and Yomitan are both GPL-3.0. The deinflect.json rule table is arguably data rather than code, but if this app is ever published, attribute it and consider whether GPL obligations attach. JMdict/JMnedict are CC BY-SA 4.0 and KANJIDIC2 is CC BY-SA 3.0 — both require attribution and share-alike; put a visible credits screen in the app.

Proper names are the dominant residual failure (トム appeared 60 times in 3,000 sentences). Do not fix this by shipping JMnedict (13.4 MB zip). Fall back to per-kanji lookup and label the token as a likely name.

The 99.3% coverage figure comes from OpenJLPT textbook example sentences, which are cleaner than real subtitles. Expect worse on ASR transcripts: no punctuation, run-on cues, filler (えーと, あの), and mis-transcribed homophones. Test the tokenizer against a real ASR cue file before trusting the reader screen.

localStorage is not a safe home for saved words. iOS Safari can evict PWA storage, and the user's saved-word list is the one thing in this app they cannot recreate. Use IndexedDB, and give them an explicit export-to-JSON/CSV button.
